title: The Ha'iyya of Ibn Abi Dawud
intro: The hadith scholar Ibn Abi Dawud set out in this ode the beliefs he had received from his teachers. Al-Ajurri heard him dictate it in Baghdad’s Rusafa Mosque on a Friday, five days before the end of Sha‘ban in 309 AH. Ibn Abi Dawud told his listeners that these were his beliefs and those of his father, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and the scholars he had known. He speaks to a single companion about the Quran, God’s attributes, the Prophet’s Companions, the life to come and what faith entails. The title comes from its rhyme letter, ha (ح), which can be heard in the closing wishes for his companion’s evenings and mornings.

translation: Hold fast to God’s rope and follow His guidance.
Shun innovation in religion, that you may prosper.
1.sharh: The image of the rope comes from Quran 3:103. The listener is asked to grasp something that will hold his weight, and to follow the guidance already given to him.

translation: Make God’s Book your rule, and the practices
handed down from His Messenger, and you will come through safely and prosper.
2.sharh: God’s Book and the Prophet’s transmitted practice give substance to the opening image. Two verbs promise the listener both escape from harm and a positive gain.

translation: Say that the speech of our King is uncreated.
The God-fearing held this belief and declared it openly.
3.sharh: The first disputed question concerns the Quran as God’s speech. The stress on speaking openly prepares for the next line, which challenges the decision to withhold a judgement.

translation: Do not withhold judgement about the Quran
as followers of Jahm did, readily accepting that position.
4.sharh: “Withhold judgement” names a particular position in the controversy over the Quran. Those holding it could call the Quran God’s speech while declining to say whether it was created. Ibn Abi Dawud associates them with followers of Jahm.

translation: Do not call the Quran you have recited a created thing.
God’s speech is made clear by uttering it.
5.sharh: When someone speaks of “my recitation”, the words can mean either the reader’s own act or the text being recited. The poet’s concern is that a claim about the first will be taken to describe God’s speech itself.

translation: Say that God will reveal Himself openly to His creatures,
as the full moon is plain to see. Your Lord is clearer.
6.sharh: The full moon is unmistakable on a clear night. The poet draws on that experience to describe the certainty with which believers will see God in the life to come.

translation: He was never begotten, and He has begotten no one.
None resembles Him. Exalted is He whom all glorify.
7.sharh: The language recalls sura 112. Placed immediately after the image of the moon, it guards the distinction between being visible and having the form or family relations of a created being.

translation: A Jahmi may deny this, but we have
an explicit report bearing out our words.
8.sharh: “This” is the promised vision of God. His answer takes the form of a hadith whose wording he regards as explicit and whose narrator he is about to name.

translation: Jarir handed down these words of Muhammad.
Say what he said of this, and you will fare well.
9.sharh: Jarir ibn Abd Allah relates that, after looking at the full moon, the Prophet spoke to his Companions about seeing their Lord. The narrator’s name lets a listener recognise the report behind the earlier image.

translation: A Jahmi may also deny His right hand.
Both His hands bestow choice gifts.
10.sharh: Ibn Abi Dawud affirms the scriptural language about God’s hand and moves straight to its action in the line. Both hands give freely, and what they give is abundance.

translation: Say that each night the Almighty descends.
How, we leave unsaid. Exalted is the One who praises Himself.
11.sharh: The destination of the descent comes in the next line. Between the verb and its destination he inserts the traditional formula “without asking how” and praise of God as the One who extols Himself.

translation: He descends to the nearest heaven, granting His bounty.
The gates of heaven part and open.
12.sharh: The “layer” is the lowest of the heavens, the one nearest the world. The opening gates lead into the invitation to pray that follows.

translation: He calls, “Will anyone seek forgiveness and find One who forgives,
or ask for good and a livelihood and be granted them?”
13.sharh: Each request carries the sound of its answer. The Arabic pairs “seeking forgiveness” with “forgiver” and “asking a gift” with “is given”, making the response audible in the request.

translation: Those who handed down this report are people whose testimony is accepted.
Those who called them liars have lost and earned reproach.
14.sharh: His defence of the account of the nightly descent turns to the people who handed it down. In dismissing it as false, he says, its critics also impugn the honesty of its transmitters.

translation: Say that the finest people after Muhammad
are his two longstanding aides, followed by Uthman.
15.sharh: The two aides are Abu Bakr and Umar. “Aides” names what they did for the Prophet in his lifetime. Uthman follows them in the order of merit that Ibn Abi Dawud gives.

translation: Fourth among them, the best of creation after those three,
is Ali, a steadfast ally of goodness who succeeds in it.
16.sharh: Ali ibn Abi Talib completes the four. Goodness is first his ally and then the means of his success. The repeated word connects a lasting attachment with what he achieves.

translation: They are indeed the company, beyond all doubt,
on noble mounts of Paradise ranging through the light.
17.sharh: The four belong to the ten Companions named together in a report promising them Paradise. Here the poet pictures them riding its finest mounts through light. The remaining six are named next.

translation: Sa’id and Sa’d, Ibn Awf and Talha,
Amir of Fihr and the much-praised al-Zubayr.
18.sharh: Sa’id and Sa’d are different men. The other abbreviated names include Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, named by his father, and Abu Ubayda, named here by his given name Amir and his descent from Fihr.

translation: Speak well of all the Companions.
Do not revile them, finding fault and cutting them down.
19.sharh: The instruction extends beyond the ten who have been singled out. Two of the Arabic verbs for an attack on someone’s reputation also describe stabbing or wounding with the hand.

translation: Revelation itself has plainly told of their merit.
In the sura of Victory there are verses praising the Companions.
20.sharh: Sura 48 speaks of God’s pleasure with those who pledged allegiance beneath the tree (48:18) and describes the people with Muhammad (48:29). These passages supply the praise on which the preceding counsel rests.

translation: Be certain of what God has decreed. It is
a pillar of the faith in all its breadth.
21.sharh: He gives a conviction a place in a building. Confidence in God’s decree is a supporting pillar, while the religion it upholds stretches out around it.

translation: Do not deny Nakir and Munkar out of ignorance,
or the Pool and the Balance. You are being counselled.
22.sharh: The two names refer to the angels who question the dead. The other images belong to the Day of Resurrection, when the Prophet’s community comes to his Pool and deeds are weighed in the Balance.

translation: Say that God, the Almighty, by His grace brings forth
from the Fire bodies like charcoal, which are cast
23.sharh: The people in the report have been burnt to charcoal. The sentence carries over the verse break, leaving the listener for a moment with the helpless bodies before revealing where they are taken.

translation: beside the river in Paradise and live by its water,
like seeds in the drift of an overflowing stream.
24.sharh: Floodwater carries small seeds in the debris it leaves on its banks, where they sprout. The change from charcoal to living shoots gives the listener a visible likeness for the restoration of the bodies.

translation: God’s Messenger intercedes for creation.
Say that punishment in the grave is a truth made plain.
25.sharh: The mention of intercession follows the account of people brought out of the Fire. The second half returns to an earlier stage of the afterlife, the interval in the grave before resurrection.

translation: Never declare those who pray unbelievers because they sin.
All of them sin, and the Lord of the Throne pardons.
26.sharh: He insists that a member of the praying community can commit a sin and remain a believer. The ending leaves room for divine pardon, since no member of that community is free of wrongdoing.

translation: Do not profess the view of the Kharijites.
It brings ruin and disgrace to whoever embraces it.
27.sharh: The particular view at issue is the expulsion of a Muslim from the faith for a grave sin. Ibn Abi Dawud identifies it with the Kharijites and describes the harm as falling on the person who adopts it.

translation: Do not be a Murji’i who trifles with his religion.
A Murji’i makes a jest of religion.
28.sharh: The argument now turns to the opposite side of the dispute. The poet objects to excluding deeds from the definition of faith. “Trifling” and “jest” convey the consequence he sees in that position.

translation: Say that faith is speech and intention
and action, plainly stated in the Prophet’s teaching.
29.sharh: What the tongue says, what the heart intends and what a person actually does all enter the definition. The third element lands just after the verse break, completing the answer to the preceding dispute.

translation: At times disobedience makes it diminish. At other times
obedience makes it grow and weigh more in the Balance.
30.sharh: If action belongs to faith, wrongdoing can diminish it and obedience can increase it. The image of a scale tipping under greater weight recalls the Balance named earlier.

translation: Set aside men’s opinions and what they say.
God’s Messenger spoke words purer and more illuminating.
31.sharh: The listener comes back to the opening rule for resolving a disagreement. Where an opinion competes with a reliable report of what the Prophet said, the poet gives the clearer, more heartening word to the Prophet.

translation: Do not join those who make a game of their religion,
and so impugn the people of hadith and disparage them.
32.sharh: The people of hadith devoted themselves to transmitting and examining reports. As in the earlier warning about the Companions, an attack on someone’s good name is pictured as a physical injury.

translation: My friend, if you hold to these beliefs all your days,
you will be well at night and in the morning.
33.sharh: “These” gathers up the separate articles of belief. Calling the listener “my friend”, he ends with the ordinary cycle of going to bed and waking again. The reciter gives that last half-line a second hearing.

1.1.2-3.head: حَبلُ اللَّه
1.1.2-3.meaning: “God’s rope”, the guidance to which a believer clings. The image occurs in Quran 3:103.

1.2.3.head: بِدعِيّ
1.2.3.meaning: Someone the author considers to have introduced an unwarranted innovation into religion.

2.1.1.head: دانَ
2.1.1.meaning: To profess something as one's belief and live by it.

2.1.4.head: السُّنَن
2.1.4.meaning: Sunan, the transmitted teachings and practices of the Prophet, including what he approved.

3.1.5.head: مَليك
3.1.5.meaning: Our sovereign. The possessive refers to God as king over those who speak.

3.2.4.head: أَفصَحَ
3.2.4.meaning: To speak out clearly and declare one's position.

4.1.5.head: الوَقف
4.1.5.meaning: Waqf, suspending judgement on whether the Quran is created. It has a particular theological sense here.

4.2.4.head: جَهم
4.2.4.meaning: Jahm ibn Safwan, after whom the Jahmiyya were named. The poet uses the name in disputes over divine speech and attributes.

4.2.5.head: أَسجَحَ
4.2.5.meaning: To give way or readily assent. Al-Badr takes it as acquiescence in the position just named.

5.1.4.head: خَلق
5.1.4.meaning: A verbal noun, “creation”, used for a created thing in the formula he rejects.

5.1.5.head: قَرَأَ
5.1.5.meaning: “I recited it.” Another textual tradition has “its recitation”. Both readings turn on the distinction between the reader’s voice and the words recited.

6.2.2.head: البَدر
6.2.2.meaning: The full moon that the Companions saw with the Prophet in Jarir’s report.

7.2.5.head: المُسَبَّح
7.2.5.meaning: The One whom people glorify and declare free of imperfection. The Arabic form is passive.

8.1.3.head: الجَهمِيّ
8.1.3.meaning: Jahmi, a follower of Jahm ibn Safwan, also a polemical label for an opponent on a particular question.

8.2.1.head: مِصداق
8.2.1.meaning: What bears out a statement or shows it to be true, here a prophetic report.

8.2.5.head: مُصَرَّح
8.2.5.meaning: Explicitly stated. The reciter opens the vowel after r here as he does in the line on faith. Al-Ajurri and the displayed verse have the active musarrih, a report that speaks clearly.

9.1.2.head: جَرير
9.1.2.meaning: Jarir ibn Abd Allah al-Bajali, the Companion who transmitted the account involving the full moon.

9.1.5.head: مُحَمَّد
9.1.5.meaning: Muhammad, the Prophet to whom Jarir traces the report.

10.2.4.head: نَفَحَ
10.2.4.meaning: To bestow something liberally, as one bestows a gift.

11.1.3.head: الجَبّار
11.1.3.meaning: Al-Jabbar, the Almighty, one of the divine names.

11.2.1-2.head: بِلا كَيف
11.2.1-2.meaning: “Without a how”, a traditional formula for affirming the report while declining to specify the manner of the descent.

11.2.5.head: المُتَمَدِّح
11.2.5.meaning: The One who declares the praise rightfully His.

12.1.2-3.head: طَبَقُ الدُّنيا
12.1.2-3.meaning: “The nearest layer”, the lowest heaven, closest to the earth.

12.1.4.head: مَنَّ
12.1.4.meaning: To confer a favour or bestow a benefit.

13.1.3.head: مُستَغفِر
13.1.3.meaning: Someone asking forgiveness. The word is answered by “forgiver” from the same Arabic root.

13.2.1.head: مُستَمنِح
13.2.1.meaning: Someone who asks a gift. The verb at the end answers the request by granting it.

14.1.4-6.meaning: “Whose report is not rejected”, transmitters whose reliability is accepted.

14.2.5.head: قُبِّحَ
14.2.5.meaning: They earned condemnation. The passive form also carries the force of a wish against them.

15.1.6.head: مُحَمَّد
15.1.6.meaning: Muhammad. The order that follows concerns the Prophet’s Companions.

15.2.1.head: وَزير
15.2.1.meaning: The Prophet’s two aides, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and Umar ibn al-Khattab. The verse identifies them by their support for him.

15.2.2.meaning: From long ago, of long standing.

15.2.4.head: عُثمان
15.2.4.meaning: Uthman ibn Affan, the third caliph.

16.1.3.head: البَرِيَّة
16.1.3.meaning: Creation, here humankind. The reciter stretches the vowel before the t, as he does in al-sahaba three lines later. It sounds close to the plural al-bariyyat. His displayed verse and the transmitted texts use the collective singular.

16.2.1.head: عَلِيّ
16.2.1.meaning: Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet’s cousin and the fourth caliph.

16.2.2-3.head: حَليفُ الخَير
16.2.2-3.meaning: “An ally of goodness”, someone who keeps as close to it as to a sworn ally.

17.1.2.head: الرَّهط
17.1.2.meaning: A company of men, here the ten Companions named together in a report promising them Paradise.

17.2.2.head: نُجُب
17.2.2.meaning: Mounts of fine breeding, particularly choice riding camels.

17.2.3.head: الفِردَوس
17.2.3.meaning: Firdaws, Paradise, also used in hadith for its highest part.

18.1.1.head: سَعيد
18.1.1.meaning: Sa'id ibn Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl, one of the ten Companions named in the report.

18.1.2.head: سَعد
18.1.2.meaning: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, also called Sa'd ibn Malik. His name differs from Sa'id in the preceding word.

18.1.3-4.head: اِبنُ عَوف
18.1.3-4.meaning: Ibn Awf, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf. The poet identifies him through his father.

18.1.5.head: طَلحَة
18.1.5.meaning: Talha ibn Ubayd Allah al-Taymi, one of the early emigrants from Mecca.

18.2.1-2.head: عامِرُ فِهر
18.2.1-2.meaning: Amir of Fihr, Abu Ubayda Amir ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Jarrah. Fihr is an ancestor of his clan.

18.2.3.head: الزُّبَير
18.2.3.meaning: Al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, son of the Prophet’s paternal aunt Safiyya.

19.2.3.head: طَعّان
19.2.3.meaning: Someone persistently given to attacking other people’s good name.

20.2.2.head: الفَتح
20.2.2.meaning: Al-Fath, Victory, sura 48 of the Quran. Verses 18 and 29 praise the Prophet’s Companions.

20.2.3.head: آي
20.2.3.meaning: Verses of the Quran. The Arabic is the shorter plural of aya.

21.2.1.head: دِعامَة
21.2.1.meaning: A supporting pillar or prop, here an image for belief in divine decree.

21.2.5.head: أَفيَح
21.2.5.meaning: Spacious, expansive, as of a landscape stretching far in every direction.

22.1.4-5.head: نَكير وَمُنكَر
22.1.4-5.meaning: Nakir and Munkar, the two angels named in hadith as questioning the dead in the grave.

22.2.2.head: الحَوض
22.2.2.meaning: Hawd, the Prophet’s Pool, to which his community comes on the Day of Resurrection.

22.2.3.head: الميزان
22.2.3.meaning: Mizan, the Balance in which deeds are weighed on the Day of Resurrection.

22.2.5.head: نُصِحَ
22.2.5.meaning: You are being given counsel. The nasal consonant before ṣ sounds close to m in this performance. The transmitted verb turns the address back to the friend receiving the advice.

23.2.5.head: الفَحم
23.2.5.meaning: Charcoal. In the underlying report the bodies have been charred by the Fire.

24.2.1.head: حِبّ
24.2.1.meaning: Seeds of plants carried by the flood that can sprout along its edge. The wording recalls the small seed in Abu Sa‘id’s account of the river of life.

24.2.2-3.head: حَميلُ السَّيل
24.2.2-3.meaning: “The flood’s burden”, the debris and silt that floodwater carries, with seeds that can then germinate.

24.2.6.head: طَفَحَ
24.2.6.meaning: To overflow or rise beyond the banks, as a river swollen by rain.

25.1.5.head: شافِع
25.1.5.meaning: An intercessor, one who asks mercy on behalf of others. The Prophet intercedes with God’s permission.

26.1.2.head: أَكفَرَ
26.1.2.meaning: To declare someone an unbeliever. The prohibition addresses judgement on a Muslim merely for committing a sin.

26.2.3-4.head: ذو العَرش
26.2.3-4.meaning: “The Lord of the Throne”, God, whose sovereignty is invoked just as pardon is mentioned.

27.1.4.head: الخَوارِج
27.1.4.meaning: Kharijites, early Muslim movements. The particular doctrine cited here is declaring the perpetrator of a grave sin an unbeliever.

28.1.3.head: مُرجِئِيّ
28.1.3.meaning: Murji'i, a member of the theological tendency known as the Murji'a. The issue in these lines is the exclusion of deeds from faith.

29.1.5.head: نِيَّة
29.1.5.meaning: Inward intention. The verse places it alongside spoken profession and outward action.

29.2.1.head: فِعل
29.2.1.meaning: Deed, the third element in the definition. The reciter says “deed” where the video card uses a synonym, “work”.

30.1.2.head: طَور
30.1.2.meaning: At one time, in alternation with “at another”.

30.2.2.head: نَمى
30.2.2.meaning: It grows, referring to faith. The reciter ends the word with an ā sound. Two other texts read yanmī and yanmū. All three describe faith increasing through obedience.

30.2.5.head: رَجَحَ
30.2.5.meaning: To tip the Balance by having greater weight.

31.2.5.head: أَشرَح
31.2.5.meaning: Clearer and more heartening, a comparative applied to the Prophet’s teaching.

32.2.3-4.head: أَهلُ الحَديث
32.2.3-4.meaning: Ahl al-hadith, the people devoted to collecting and examining prophetic reports, also the name of a theological tradition.

32.2.5.head: قَدَحَ
32.2.5.meaning: To impugn a person’s standing or reliability.

33.1.6.meaning: “My friend”, a shortened form of address with the last consonant of sahib dropped.
